description: Physical, logical and secure-destruction measures, plus five Acts every IT professional must understand.
hero_image_caption: A biometric fingerprint scanner controlling access to a secure server room.
content_html:
Why Prevention Matters

Knowing about cyber-security threats (from Lesson 5) is only half the picture. The other half is knowing how to stop them. Prevention measures fall into three categories: physical (controlling access to devices and buildings), logical (software-based controls) and secure destruction (safely disposing of data and devices). Each reduces a different kind of risk.

Physical Prevention Measures

Physical measures stop unauthorised people from reaching hardware in the first place. Biometric devices (fingerprint scanners, retina readers, facial recognition systems) grant access only to enrolled individuals — they are difficult to forge and eliminate the need for keys that can be lost or copied. Keypads require a PIN code to enter a secured area — quick to use but vulnerable if someone watches the code being entered (shoulder surfing). RFID (Radio-Frequency Identification) is used in staff ID cards that grant access by being held near a reader — cards can be cloned if not properly protected. Firewalls in hardware form are dedicated devices placed between a network and the internet, inspecting all traffic and blocking suspicious data packets. Secure backups (physical offsite copies) ensure data can be recovered if hardware is damaged, stolen or destroyed.

Logical Prevention Measures

Logical prevention measures are enforced by software. Access rights and permissions ensure users can only view, edit or delete the files their role requires — a call-centre agent should not be able to access payroll files. Anti-virus and anti-malware software scans for known malware patterns and quarantines or removes threats. Usernames and passwords are the most basic logical control: they should be complex (mixed case, numbers, symbols) and unique per account.

Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second layer: even if an attacker obtains a password, they also need the one-time code sent to the user’s phone. Encryption scrambles data in transit and at rest, so that intercepted data is useless without the decryption key. Secure backups in logical form means keeping encrypted digital copies in a separate location — automated cloud backups are a common approach. Software firewalls monitor incoming and outgoing traffic on a single device, blocking suspicious connections.

When a device is retired or sold, simply deleting files is not enough — data can be recovered from a “deleted” drive using widely available software. Four named methods ensure data cannot be recovered. Data erasure overwrites every storage location with random data multiple times, leaving no trace of the originals. Data sanitation is a broader process of clearing a storage medium to a certified standard, often including overwriting and verification that nothing remains. Magnetic wipe (degaussing) uses a powerful magnet to disrupt the magnetic patterns on a traditional hard drive, rendering data unreadable — it does not work on SSDs or USB drives. Physical destruction (shredding, crushing or melting the storage medium) is the most absolute method; it is typically used for drives containing highly sensitive data where recovery must be provably impossible.

Key Fact

Physical measures (biometric devices, keypads, RFID, firewalls, secure backups) prevent unauthorised physical access. Logical measures (access rights, anti-virus, 2FA, encryption, firewalls, passwords, secure backups) prevent unauthorised software access. Secure destruction (data erasure, sanitation, magnetic wipe, physical destruction) ensures data on retired devices cannot be recovered.

IT Legislation — Five Acts to Know

The exam requires knowledge of five Acts: what each one makes illegal or requires, who it protects, and its implications for data, individuals and organisations. Detailed knowledge of specific sections or clause numbers is not required. Treat each Act at the level of purpose and implications.

The Computer Misuse Act creates three criminal offences: (1) accessing a computer without authorisation, (2) accessing a computer with intent to commit a further crime, and (3) modifying computer data without authorisation (e.g. installing malware). It protects individuals and organisations from hackers and malware creators. The implication for organisations: they should maintain logs of access attempts to detect and prove unauthorised access.

The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act protects original creative work — including software, images, music and written content — from being copied or distributed without permission. For IT, this means you cannot legally copy software, use images from the web without a licence, or resell a software product you did not create. Organisations must ensure they have valid licences for all software they use.

The Data Protection Act governs how organisations collect, store, use and share personal data. Organisations must have a lawful reason for holding data, keep it accurate and secure, not retain it longer than necessary, and give individuals the right to access or correct their data. Failure to comply can result in regulatory fines. This Act directly supports cyber-security by requiring organisations to secure personal data against unauthorised access.

The Freedom of Information Act gives the public the right to request information held by public bodies (government departments, schools, NHS trusts, local councils). Public bodies must respond within 20 working days. For IT, this means public sector organisations must store records in accessible formats and must have systems in place to locate, retrieve and release information on request — while withholding genuinely exempt information (such as commercially sensitive or personal data).

The Health and Safety at Work Act requires employers to provide a safe working environment. In IT contexts, this includes: positioning screens to reduce glare, providing ergonomic chairs and keyboards to prevent repetitive strain injury, ensuring cables are managed to prevent tripping hazards, and offering regular breaks from screen use. Employees also have a responsibility to use equipment safely.

Key Fact

The five Acts: Computer Misuse Act (unauthorised computer access illegal), Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (protects creative works from copying), Data Protection Act (governs personal data handling), Freedom of Information Act (public right to access public-body information), Health and Safety at Work Act (employer duty to provide safe IT working environment).
exam_tip_html: Legislation questions most often use the command word “describe” or “explain”. For a 3-mark “explain” answer, state the purpose of the Act, explain what it requires an organisation to do, and link it to the scenario. For example: “The Data Protection Act requires organisations to keep personal data secure [purpose]; this means the hospital must encrypt patient records and restrict access to authorised staff only [requirement]; if they fail to do this, they could face a regulatory fine and patients could have their medical data stolen [implication].” Never write detailed clause numbers — the spec explicitly excludes detailed knowledge of the legislation.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prevention measures split into physical (biometrics, keypads, RFID, hardware firewalls, backups), logical (access rights, anti-virus, 2FA, encryption, passwords, software firewalls, backups) and secure destruction (data erasure, sanitation, magnetic wipe, physical destruction).
  • The five Acts in scope: Computer Misuse Act, Copyright Designs and Patents Act, Data Protection Act, Freedom of Information Act, Health and Safety at Work Act. Know the purpose and implications for data, individuals and organisations — not the detailed legal clauses.
  • Legislation supports cyber-security by creating legal duties: organisations that fail to protect data face regulatory fines; individuals who access systems without permission commit criminal offences.

practice_questions.text: Which prevention measure requires a user to provide both a password and a one-time code sent to their phone before they can log in?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Two-factor authentication (2FA) (only). Distractors: encryption (scrambles data, does not authenticate users), biometric device (uses biological features, not a code), access rights (controls what data a user can see after login).

practice_questions.text: Identify one logical prevention measure that protects against malware.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: anti-virus/anti-malware software (only). Do not accept encryption or 2FA (these protect data and accounts, not directly against malware detection).

practice_questions.text: Outline the purpose of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act in an IT context.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: the Act protects original creative works (including software, images and music) (1) from being copied, distributed or used without the creator's permission, requiring organisations to hold valid software licences (1). Award 1 mark for identifying protection of creative works without specifying the IT context.

practice_questions.text: Describe how encryption is used as a logical prevention measure to protect data.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: encryption converts data into an unreadable format (ciphertext) using a key (1); this means that even if the data is intercepted in transit or stolen at rest, an attacker without the decryption key cannot read it (1). Award 1 mark for stating that encryption makes data unreadable without explaining the key mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Data Protection Act supports an organisation's cyber-security measures.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): states what the Data Protection Act requires (organisations must collect, store and secure personal data lawfully and protect it from unauthorised access) (1); explains the link to cyber-security (this legally obliges organisations to implement security controls such as encryption and access restrictions, because failure to secure data can result in a breach) (1); links to consequence (organisations that do not comply face regulatory fines and reputational damage, so the law creates a financial incentive to invest in cyber-security measures) (1).
Secure (2): requirement stated and linked to security, but consequence or link to cyber-security is underdeveloped.
Developing (1): Act named and purpose stated without linking to cyber-security.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether logical prevention measures alone are sufficient to protect an organisation's data from cyber-security threats.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): detailed analysis of the strengths of logical measures (e.g. encryption protects data even if a device is physically stolen; 2FA prevents unauthorised login even when passwords are compromised; anti-virus removes known malware threats automatically); analysis of limitations (e.g. logical measures cannot prevent a determined attacker who has physical access — if someone steals a server, encryption must already be in place before the theft, and if they also steal the decryption key or the logged-in device, encryption is defeated; zero-day malware not yet in anti-virus databases will bypass anti-virus software; human error in setting access rights can still leave data exposed); analysis of how physical measures complement logical ones (physical barriers such as biometric access and RFID prevent attackers from reaching hardware; secure destruction prevents data recovery from retired devices); justified conclusion (e.g. logical measures are essential but insufficient alone — a layered approach combining physical, logical and procedural controls provides the strongest protection).
Secure (5–7): both sides addressed with some development; conclusion present but not fully justified.
Developing (3–4): logical measures described with some limitations noted; one-sided.
Emerging (1–2): vague awareness that both types of measure exist; no analysis.
0: no creditworthy content.

knowledge_checks.q: Which secure destruction method uses a powerful magnet to render data on a traditional hard drive unreadable?
Which Act gives members of the public the right to request information held by public bodies such as schools and government departments?
options: Health and Safety at Work Act

knowledge_checks.q: _____ converts data into an unreadable ciphertext format, so that intercepted data is useless to an attacker without the correct key.
The Computer Misuse Act makes it a criminal offence to access a computer system _____.
Match each prevention measure to its category.
right: Logical — adds a second proof-of-identity layer beyond a password
Secure destruction — renders hard drive data unreadable using a magnet
Physical — grants access using unique biological characteristics
Logical — scrambles data so intercepted content cannot be read

flashcard_questions.a: Security devices that use biological features like fingerprints or retina scans to grant access.
A login method requiring two forms of ID — typically a password plus a one-time code.
Converting data into unreadable ciphertext using a key so it cannot be read if intercepted.

flashcard_questions.q: What is RFID used for in physical security?
flashcard_questions.a: Staff ID cards grant building or room access when held near a reader.
Data erasure, data sanitation, magnetic wipe, physical destruction.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Computer Misuse Act make illegal?
flashcard_questions.a: Unauthorised access to computer systems and unauthorised modification of data.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Data Protection Act require organisations to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Collect, store and secure personal data lawfully and give individuals rights over their data.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Freedom of Information Act give the public?
flashcard_questions.a: The right to request information held by public bodies, who must respond within 20 working days.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the Health and Safety at Work Act apply in IT workplaces?
flashcard_questions.a: Employers must provide safe working conditions including ergonomic equipment and screen break guidelines.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is simply deleting a file not considered secure destruction?
flashcard_questions.a: Deleted files can be recovered using widely available software — secure methods overwrite or destroy the medium.

glossary_terms.definition: Security devices that identify individuals using unique biological characteristics such as fingerprints, retina scans or facial recognition to grant or deny access.
Radio-frequency identification — a system that uses radio waves to read data from a chip embedded in a card or tag, used for access control and asset tracking.
Software-based controls that protect IT systems and data, including access rights, anti-virus software, encryption, firewalls and two-factor authentication.

A security method that requires a user to provide two separate forms of identification before access is granted — typically something they know (password) plus something they have (a code sent to a phone).
The process of converting data into an unreadable format (ciphertext) using a key, so that only authorised parties with the correct key can read it.
A UK law that makes unauthorised access to computer systems, unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence, and unauthorised modification of computer material criminal offences.
A UK law that protects original creative works (software, music, images, video) from being copied, distributed or used without the creator's permission.
UK law (incorporating UK GDPR principles) that sets rules for how personal data must be collected, stored, processed and shared — giving individuals rights over their own data.
